The leiqin is a Chinese bowed string instrument, a chordophone by sounding classification. Its body is made of brass and wood and covered with snakeskin, with a long fingerboard without frets; two strings cross a small bridge set near the upper edge of the snakeskin and are held by a movable part. It is played sitting down with the body on the leg, the instrument upright or nearly upright; unlike instruments of the huqin family such as the erhu, the strings are stopped on the fingerboard in the manner of the sanxian. The Shandong traditional folk musician Wang Dianyu created it by adapting the zhuihu in the late 1920s.
演奏者坐姿，琴身置於腿上，琴桿垂直或近垂直。以弓拉奏兩弦，弦經蛇皮上的小琴橋，由: The player sits with the body on the leg and the neck vertical or nearly vertical. The bow draws across the two strings, which pass over a small bridge on the snakeskin and are held by a movable part, the shankou. The strings are stopped by touching them against the fingerboard, in the same way as the sanxian and unlike huqin such as the erhu. A beginner can use a wooden leg rest with a smooth underside to steady the instrument and control the pressure of stopping.
